title: We Tested 11 Automatic Cat Feeders: These Are the Ones That Actually Deliver
summary:
If your cat has ever treated your face like a breakfast buffet at dawn, you know the struggle. Automatic cat feeders promise liberation, but not all are created equal. WIRED put 11 models through their paces, and the results reveal a new generation of smart feeders that go way beyond kibble on a timer.

The standout for dry food is the Petkit YumShare Dual-Hopper 2 ($170). It features a dual hopper for two food types, a crystal-clear 1080p camera with night vision, and—crucially—AI that analyzes remaining food in the bowl to prevent overfeeding. The app lets you schedule meals, dispense snacks, and even talk to your cat via two-way audio. No subscription is needed for the AI, which can recognize up to 20 individual pets and log their meals.

For wet food, the Petlibro Polar Smart Wet Feeder ($170) is a game-changer. It's essentially a thermoelectric mini-fridge that keeps food at or below 50°F, pausing cooling 30 minutes before mealtime to serve it at the ideal temperature. The three stainless steel bowls are wide and shallow to prevent whisker fatigue and feline acne. A sensor ensures the lid doesn't close while your cat is eating. Our tester loved it so much they bought a second one.

Budget-conscious buyers aren't left out. The Petlibro Granary Camera Feeder ($100) offers a reliable app, HD camera, and customizable meal plans. The Petlibro Air Feeder ($60) is a sleek, no-frills option with a rechargeable battery and tiny portion sizes for snack control. Even the Oneisall 2-in-1 Dual Feeder ($50) gets the job done, though its app can be buggy.

Whether you're managing a greedy eater, a picky nibbler, or just want to sleep past sunrise, the right automatic feeder can be a small revolution. Your cat might still rule the house, but at least you'll get to set the breakfast schedule.
why_it_matters: As more households treat pets as family with busy work schedules, these smart feeders don't just offer convenience—they address real health issues like obesity and dental problems, and raise important questions about how much technology should be involved in caring for a living animal.

background_read: Automatic pet feeders have been around for decades, but early models were simple timers that dumped kibble into a bowl at set hours, often jamming or dispensing too much. The rise of smart home tech has turned them into Wi-Fi-connected devices with cameras, apps, and even machine learning.

Petkit and Petlibro are two leading Chinese brands in the smart pet market, competing with Western companies by offering advanced features like app-controlled feeding and pet recognition at lower prices. WIRED is a tech and culture magazine known for its in-depth product reviews.

Veterinarians warn that cats fed only dry food may not get enough moisture, which is why wet food feeders are gaining attention. However, leaving wet food out too long at room temperature can cause bacterial growth, a problem the Petlibro Polar addresses with active cooling.

perspectives.description: These devices let owners stay at work late or sleep in without guilt, and the portion control and fresh food options can actually improve a cat's diet. Video and AI features provide peace of mind and even fun interactions while away from home.

Relying too heavily on automatic feeders might cause owners to miss early signs of illness that are caught during routine manual feeding. Additionally, internet-connected cameras inside the home always carry some risk of unauthorized access or data collection by manufacturers.

The pet tech industry is mirroring human smart home trends: subscription-free AI, eco-friendly materials, and integration with other devices. However, the real differentiator is whether these products actually solve specific animal welfare issues like whisker fatigue, rather than just adding flashy features.

The next step might be feeders that sync with veterinary records or use image recognition to spot changes in weight, coat, or eating habits and alert owners. As AI improves, these devices could become proactive health monitors, but that raises ethical questions about giving too much caregiving responsibility to machines.
